unmatched_gen: The malaria parasite's chloroquine resistance transporter is a member of the drug/metabolite transporter superfamily.
The malaria parasite's chloroquine resistance transporter (CRT) is an integral membrane protein localized to the parasite's acidic digestive vacuole.
Mutations in CRT can cause a decreased intravacuolar concentration of chloroquine and thereby confer chloroquine resistance.
The mechanism by which mutations in CRT confer chloroquine resistance is not understood.

Comparisons between CRT and other members of the superfamily provide insight into the possible role of the protein and into the significance of the mutations associated with the chloroquine resistance phenotype.
The key chloroquine-resistance-conferring mutation (K76T) is localized in a region of the protein implicated in substrate selectivity.

The K76T mutation is predicted to alter the selectivity of the protein such that it is able to transport the cationic (protonated) form of chloroquine down its steep concentration gradient, out of the acidic vacuole, and therefore away from its site of action.
